messages.subject: Slow Warmup with multivariate model in Rstan 2.0
parts:
Hi everyone,

I recieved the news of the last version of Stan and Rstan and I can not report any issue in regarding to the installation/update of these softwares with my GNU/Debian.

Just for check I try some multivariate models but felt some big differences related to the initialization process!

In the 1.3 version I always recieve the warning already mentioned in the mailing list of the Metropolis Rejected and non symmetric matrix... thread "Positive definiteness failure on initialization causes crash rather than rejection". However after some few notice per each chain the model run very fast.

Now I have great difficults to make the things work. The same model that was running in just 10 minutes with the last version, now are in the warmup for 2 hours. And the warning is not appearing.

I need to mention that I was recieving another warning. Due to implementation trick, learn here in the mailing list, thread "Multivariate Coefficients" I am inputing a sampling statement with the function col(). Then the warning tell me the it is a transformation nad must to increment the lp__.

It is actually a transformation?

Perhaps, this difficulty to start the sampling process can happen because of this "transformation" with the increment of lp__?

I am open to send the entire source code and data set if it is need!

Thank you indeed for any reply.

Cheers,
FH

Daniel,

Thank indeed for your instant reply.

As requested I am forwarding the entire code and the data set is attached.

rm(list = ls()); ls() # clean WorkSpace

## requiring and setting
require(rstan) # interface R/Stan/C++ 'HMC'
set_cppo('fast') # fast optimization

## reading data
dataSet <- read.table('dataSet.txt'
                      header = TRUE,
                      sep = '\t',
                      dec = ',')

dataSet$entry <- factor(dataSet$entry) 
y <- subset(dataSet, select = c('Pe', 'G', 'V'))
N <- nrow(y)
P <- ncol(y)
T <- nlevels(dataSet$entry)
X <- model.matrix(~ entry - 1, data = dataSet)
Omega <- diag(P) * c(.001, 1000, 200)
mu0 <- apply(y, 2, mean)

## input list to Stan
StanData <- list(y = y, # data matrix
                 N = N, # number of observations
                 P = P, # number of traits
                 T = T, # number of levels
                 X = X, # incidence matrix
                 Omega = Omega, # priori for Wishart
                 mu0 = mu0) # priori for mu

## Source Code
sourceCode <- "
data {
   int<lower=0> N;
   int<lower=0> P;
   int<lower=0> T;
   vector[ P ] y[ N ];
   vector[ T ] X[ N ];
   vector[ P ] mu0;
   cov_matrix[ P ] Omega;
}
transformed data {
   real nu;
   nu <- P * ( P + 1.0 ) / 2.0;
}
parameters {
   matrix[ P, T ] alpha;
   cov_matrix[ P ] Gen;
   cov_matrix[ P ] Res;
}
transformed parameters {
   vector[ P ] mu[ N ];
   for ( p in 1:P )
         for ( n in 1:N )
            mu[ n, p ] <- dot_product( X[ n ], alpha[ p ] );
}
model {
  Gen ~ inv_wishart( nu, Omega );
   for ( t in 1:T )
     col( alpha, t ) ~ multi_normal( mu0, Gen );
  Res ~ inv_wishart( nu, Omega );
  for ( n in 1:N )
     y[ n ] ~ multi_normal( mu[ n ], Res );
}
"

## translating, compiling, dyn.load and sampling
fit <- stan(model_code = sourceCode, # compiled code
            data = StanData, # data input
            init = 'random', # != seeds p/ cade
            chain = 2, # chain number
            iter = 2E4, # run length
            warmup = 2E3, # like the burn-in
            thin = 20, # between samples
            pars = 'Gen') # monitor

## summary
print(fit, digits = 4)

Best Regards,
FH

parts:
I've recreated the issue as well.

On the bright side, at least both versions got the same answer.

The timing doesn't look so good for Stan 2.0. This was measured
just with split R-hat in a single chain with random inits in (-2,2).
1000 warmup iterations, 1000 sampling iterations.

Stan 1.3 Stan 2.0
time: 1m 32m
mean tree depth: 3 1
step size: 1.4 2e-4
approx med R-hat: 700 10
accept stat: ? 0.7

It seems like the effective sample size issue must be due to warmup.

But because Stan 2 is actually doing fewer leapfrog iterations (1 vs. 8),
I think something must have also slowed down one of the multivariate
distributions. Tomorrow, or over the weekend, I'll run some
profiling on it to see if anything pops up on the code efficiency
front.

In looking at the parameters, they have pretty widely varying scales.
For instance, one of the mean vectors fits to

mu[71,1] 0.2
mu[71,2] 73.7
mu[71,3] 33.4

The alpha parameters are similarly widely scaled (factor of several hundred).

I tried a run with

sample adapt delta=0.95

hoping that would push down the step size and increase the tree depth, but all it
did was push the stepsize down to 7.5e-5 and make n_eff even lower; tree depth remained
at 1. Setting delta=0.1 helped with effective sample size and speed, but didn't
change the tree depth away from 1.

- Bob

This is in line with what we've been seeing elsewhere. These
histograms make things much clearer in terms of what's going
on than means and deviations.

Something in 2.0 is more conservative about step sizes
and thus leads to deeper trees. Hopefully that will
lead to more effective samples/second. It should lead
to more robust inferences in problematic models (I have
some latent logistic models which 2.0 runs much better
than 1.3 for just this reason).

The depth is log2 of the number of leapfrog steps taken.
If there are 0, the right answer is -infinity, but we
didn't want to mess up things like means if there was just
a single 0 steps. What we should be doing is reporting
+1 on this, I think.

I'm taking it up on the dev list and added a note to our manual
issue tracker to make sure to add an explanation in the next version
of the manual.

> Maybe this is deviating from the original problem towards properties of my model, but what are those -1's and accept

You'll see that the deep tree depths are when step sizes are
low and shallow tree depths are when step sizes are high.

We think what's going on in 2.0 is that step size is getting
shrunk too agressively.

> Sounds a bit unhealthy. :) (I need to get familiar with NUTS.)

iterations per second. Is that similar from 1.3 to 2.0?
> Traceplots look good but have a couple of periods of stuckiness across all parameters.

If chains are getting stuck, you can try adding
stepsize_jitter. The lower step sizes should get it unstuck (at
the expense of more time --- but it should be a win overall in
effective samples/second).
